strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: converting panoramic generation/perception into graphics-ready 3D scene assets with geometry and PBR-like material maps, which is relevant for immersive scene generation, simulation, and rendering workflows.

The proposed OmniX formulation is appealingly unified. Reusing a pretrained flow-matching model with modality-specific LoRA/adapters for image-to-panorama generation, panorama-to-X perception, and masked completion is a practical design with clear extensibility.

PanoX is a useful dataset contribution for a comparatively under-served setting: panoramic RGB with aligned distance, normals, albedo, roughness, and metallic annotations across indoor and outdoor synthetic scenes. The dataset comparison motivates this gap well.

The experimental results for panoramic perception are strong. OmniX substantially improves over compared intrinsic decomposition methods on PanoX-OutDomain, and the geometry results are competitive, especially for normal estimation and detail preservation.

The ablations are meaningful: adapter-structure comparisons support the Separate-Adapter design, and the camera-ray and joint material/geometry modeling studies give useful insight rather than only reporting a single final model.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with helpful pipeline figures and qualitative examples showing how perception outputs feed into reconstruction, relighting, and physical simulation.
weaknesses: The central graphics-ready 3D scene claim is only weakly evaluated. The relighting, free-exploration, and physics demonstrations are qualitative screenshots/videos, with no quantitative assessment of mesh quality, material accuracy under novel lighting, simulation validity, rendering artifacts, or user/task-based evaluation.

PanoX appears relatively small and scene-limited despite the large instance count: it is based on only 8 large-scale scenes, with 6 split into train/val/test segments and 2 held out. This raises concern that performance may rely on limited synthetic scene diversity and may not transfer broadly to real panoramas.

The evaluation is heavily synthetic. In-the-wild results are qualitative only, so the paper does not convincingly establish real-world robustness, especially for difficult material properties such as metallicity, which the authors themselves note generalizes poorly.

The comparisons may not be fully conclusive. Several baselines are not designed for panoramas or PBR panoramic material estimation, and it is unclear whether all were adapted, calibrated, or fine-tuned under equally favorable conditions. Some missing metrics for competitors, especially normals/depth for methods that do not output them directly, make the tables harder to interpret.

Panorama generation and completion are under-evaluated. The paper provides qualitative examples but lacks standard or task-specific metrics for image-to-panorama quality, completion consistency, seam artifacts, diversity, or 3D consistency.

Technical novelty is moderate. The framework is a sensible adaptation of pretrained FLUX/DiT models with LoRA and cross-modal adapters, but many ingredients are inherited from existing diffusion/flow, adapter, panorama lifting, and mesh projection pipelines. The contribution is more integrative than fundamentally new.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. Important implementation choices such as training steps, LoRA ranks, adapter parameter counts, sampling/inference settings, mask distributions, dataset release status/licensing, and compute/runtime details are either missing or only briefly described.

The method inherits substantial limitations: slow training/inference, seam handling via a heuristic horizontal blending technique, bumpy reconstructed surfaces from imperfect distance prediction, and weak metallic generalization. These directly affect the claimed downstream graphics-readiness.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: using panoramic generation and perception to produce 3D scenes that are more usable in graphics pipelines than appearance-only 2D lifting methods.
The proposed scope is ambitious, covering image-to-panorama generation, panoramic RGB-to-X perception, masked completion, and downstream mesh/PBR workflows in a single adapter-based framework.

PanoX is a potentially useful dataset contribution because it includes panoramic RGB, geometry, albedo, roughness, and metallic annotations across indoor and outdoor synthetic scenes, a combination not well covered by existing resources.

The quantitative results on PanoX-OutDomain show clear gains for intrinsic/PBR prediction over several compared methods, and the adapter ablations provide some evidence that the separate-adapter design is preferable to simpler concatenation/shared-adapter variants.
weaknesses: The central claims are much broader than the evidence. The paper claims graphics-ready 3D scenes suitable for PBR rendering, relighting, simulation, and exploration, but the evaluation of these capabilities is almost entirely qualitative and limited to small demonstrations. There is no quantitative assessment of mesh quality, relighting correctness, material physical plausibility, collision/simulation reliability, or navigability.

The dataset is described as large-scale, but it appears to contain only 8 underlying 3D scenes. Even with 10k panorama instances, this raises serious concerns about scene diversity, overfitting to renderer/domain artifacts, and whether PanoX-OutDomain is a meaningful proxy for real generalization, since it is still synthetic and apparently from the same data-generation process.

The comparisons are not fully convincing. Many baselines were designed for perspective images, videos, or different inverse-rendering settings, while OmniX is trained on PanoX/Structured3D and evaluated on PanoX-OutDomain. The paper does not clearly establish that baselines are adapted, fine-tuned, prompted, scaled, or postprocessed under equally favorable conditions.

The generation and completion parts are under-evaluated. Image-to-panorama and masked completion results are shown visually, but there are no quantitative metrics, baselines, user studies, consistency checks, or failure analyses. These are major components of the claimed unified framework, so the evidentiary gap is substantial.

The method novelty is incremental relative to existing diffusion/flow adaptation practices: the unified formulation is mostly a restatement of conditional flow matching, and the main architectural contribution is a LoRA/cross-modal adapter organization. The paper does not provide enough analysis to show deeper algorithmic insight beyond empirical adapter selection.

Important implementation and reproducibility details are missing or underspecified, including LoRA ranks, exact adapter insertion points, training steps, inference/sampling settings, mask-generation parameters, dataset licensing/release plan, and how all baselines were run. This makes it difficult to reproduce or audit the reported gains.

The paper acknowledges serious limitations that directly affect the main application claims: distance predictions are not accurate enough and lead to bumpy surfaces, metallic prediction generalizes poorly, and 2D generative priors may have limited value for PBR material estimation. These limitations are not resolved by the experiments.

Overall, while the direction is interesting and the synthetic benchmark/results have merit, the scientific case is not yet strong enough for acceptance at ECCV because the main graphics-ready scene-generation claims are not rigorously validated and the experimental setup leaves major fairness and generalization questions open.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: moving panorama-based 2D lifting beyond appearance-only scene generation toward geometry and PBR material prediction suitable for graphics workflows. This is a meaningful contribution for computer vision, graphics, and embodied simulation use cases.

OmniX is a coherent framework that unifies image-to-panorama generation, panorama-to-X perception, masked completion, and guided perception through lightweight modality-specific adapters on top of a strong pre-trained flow-matching model. The formulation is practical and extensible, even if the algorithmic novelty is moderate.

The proposed PanoX dataset is valuable: panoramic RGB with aligned distance, normals, albedo, roughness, and metallic maps across indoor and outdoor scenes fills a real gap in existing datasets. The dataset/benchmark contribution strengthens the paper substantially.

The experimental results are generally strong. OmniX substantially outperforms prior intrinsic decomposition methods on PanoX-OutDomain for albedo, roughness, and metallic estimation, and it achieves competitive geometry estimation, including notably better normal estimation than the compared baselines.

The ablations are useful and support key design choices, especially the Separate-Adapter architecture over shared-branch/shared-adapter variants. The additional discussion of joint material and joint geometry modeling is informative rather than just celebratory.

The paper is clearly written overall, with good visual examples and a candid limitations section acknowledging slow inference/training, imperfect distance prediction, bumpy geometry, and weak metallic generalization.
weaknesses: The evidence for the central claim of producing truly graphics-ready 3D scenes is still mostly qualitative. The Blender demonstrations for free exploration, relighting, and physical simulation are compelling, but there is no quantitative evaluation of mesh quality, relighting correctness, physical plausibility, collision behavior, or downstream usability compared with prior 3D scene generation systems.

The dataset scale and diversity are somewhat limited despite the large number of rendered panoramas: PanoX is derived from only 8 large-scale scenes. This raises concerns about scene/layout/material diversity, especially for generalization to real-world panoramas. The paper also has a confusing statement that the split is over “six PanoX scenes” after saying the dataset contains 8 scenes, with two used as out-domain.

Most quantitative evaluations are on synthetic data. In-the-wild performance is shown qualitatively only, so the real-domain robustness of albedo, roughness, metallic, and geometry prediction remains uncertain. This is especially important because the intended applications depend on real image-to-scene creation.

Some comparisons may be imperfectly matched. Several baselines are narrow-FoV or video/inverse-rendering methods not designed for ERP panoramas, while OmniX is trained on the proposed panoramic data. The paper would be stronger with more discussion of whether baselines were adapted or fine-tuned under comparable data conditions.

Panoramic generation and completion are under-evaluated. The paper provides qualitative examples but lacks quantitative metrics, user studies, or comparisons to panorama generation/completion baselines, despite these being part of the unified framework and 3D construction pipeline.

The method relies heavily on FLUX.1-dev and multiple task-specific adapters, so the conceptual novelty is less strong than the system/dataset contribution. Reproducibility details are also incomplete: the manuscript does not clearly state whether PanoX, code, trained adapters, prompts, and rendering/evaluation scripts will be released.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: using 2D generative priors to produce panoramic representations with geometry and PBR-related intrinsic properties, enabling downstream 3D scene construction rather than only RGB panorama synthesis.

OmniX is a coherent unified framework for panorama generation, perception, and completion. The combination of modality-specific LoRA adapters with a flow-matching backbone is practical and flexible across RGB, distance, normal, albedo, roughness, and metallic outputs.

The circular synchronization idea is technically appealing: adapting convolution and RoPE attention behavior to respect horizontal circularity is a clean way to address equirectangular seam artifacts, and the qualitative comparison against circular blending and latent rotation is convincing.

The proposed PanoX dataset addresses a real data gap by providing synthetic panoramic RGB, geometry, and material annotations across indoor and outdoor scenes. Even if limited in diversity, it is a useful benchmark-style contribution for panoramic intrinsic perception.

The experiments are fairly broad, covering panorama generation, intrinsic decomposition, geometry estimation, completion, ablations on adapter design and pretraining, and qualitative Blender demonstrations. The reported gains for intrinsic decomposition are especially strong, e.g. substantially better albedo/roughness/metallic PSNR and LPIPS than the compared methods on PanoX-OutDomain.

The paper is generally well organized and readable, with clear diagrams of the framework, adapter variants, and circular synchronization mechanism. The limitations section is candid about slow inference/training, imperfect distance estimates, and weak metallic generalization.
weaknesses: The contribution is closer to an Applied/Systems plus Datasets/Benchmarks paper than a purely Algorithms/General paper. This is not inherently negative, but the manuscript frames broad algorithmic and graphics-ready 3D claims while much of the novelty comes from integrating existing flow models, LoRA adapters, synthetic data, and known circular padding ideas. The assessment therefore depends heavily on the strength of empirical validation.

The evidence for 'graphics-ready' 3D scenes is mostly qualitative. The Blender demonstrations are interesting, but there is no quantitative evaluation of reconstructed mesh quality, relighting correctness, physical simulation validity, surface smoothness, geometry consistency across iterative completion, or comparison to 3D scene generation/reconstruction baselines on the final 3D asset quality.

PanoX appears relatively small and narrow for the scope of the claims: about 10k instances from only eight synthetic environments, with six scenes used for train/validation/test splits and two for out-of-domain testing. This raises concerns about scene diversity, synthetic bias, and whether the strong intrinsic results transfer to real panoramas beyond selected qualitative examples.

Some experimental claims are overstated. For panorama generation, OmniX is not uniformly best on SUN360: CubeDiff has better FID and FAED, while OmniX is best on KID, CLIP-FID, and CLIP score. Similarly, for geometry, OmniX is clearly behind MoGe on distance metrics, despite the paper emphasizing its overall advantage; the limitations acknowledge distance errors but the main text could be more balanced.

Baseline fairness and adaptation details need more clarity. It is not always clear whether competing intrinsic and geometry methods are evaluated zero-shot, retrained, fine-tuned, or adapted to panorama inputs with comparable data. For video or narrow-FoV methods, choices such as panorama-to-frame rendering, stitching, and preprocessing can strongly affect results.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a system of this complexity. The paper gives optimizer and resolution settings, but lacks many practical details: exact training schedules/steps, LoRA ranks and target modules, circular attention padding sizes used in final experiments, data licenses/filtering for all panorama sources, captioning prompts, normalization of modalities, candidate/inference settings, and details of the iterative completion pipeline.

The ablation study supports adapter design and pretraining, but the circular synchronization analysis is mainly qualitative. A seam-specific quantitative metric or user study would better substantiate the claim that the structural modification guarantees or consistently improves seamless generation without harming fidelity.

The material prediction task, especially metallic, is inherently difficult and the authors note poor generalization. Since PBR-readiness depends strongly on these properties, the paper should more directly evaluate physical/material plausibility rather than relying mainly on pixel-level PSNR/LPIPS against synthetic ground truth.

The method is likely computationally expensive: it trains 12 adapter models on top of Flux.1-dev and uses iterative completion for scene construction, but runtime, memory, training cost, and inference latency are not reported in enough detail for readers to judge practicality.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: turning panorama generation/perception into graphics-ready 3D assets with geometry and PBR material channels, which is relevant to vision, graphics, simulation, and embodied AI.
The submission has a broad system scope, covering image-to-panorama generation, panorama perception, completion, and an application pipeline for mesh construction, relighting, and simple simulation.

PanoX, despite limitations, is a potentially useful synthetic panorama dataset because it includes aligned RGB, distance, normals, albedo, roughness, and metallic maps across indoor and outdoor scenes.

The quantitative tables report strong gains for intrinsic-property prediction on PanoX/Structured3D and competitive panorama generation results versus recent baselines, suggesting that pre-trained 2D flow models can transfer usefully to panoramic tasks.

The ablations on adapter structure and pretrained initialization are helpful and support the claim that modality-specific adapters and pretrained image priors matter for the reported perception tasks.
weaknesses: The claimed contribution is substantially overextended. The paper presents OmniX as a unified framework, but in practice it trains 12 separate adapter models for different tasks/modalities. This weakens the unification claim and makes the method closer to a collection of task-specific LoRA adaptations around FLUX than a single general model.

The novelty is limited relative to the breadth of the claims. Circular padding/attention for equirectangular wrap-around and modality-specific LoRA adapters are sensible engineering choices, but the paper does not provide enough conceptual or empirical evidence that they constitute a major advance beyond existing panorama diffusion and adapter-based multimodal conditioning methods.

The central “graphics-ready” claim is not convincingly evaluated. The 3D scene construction, PBR relighting, free exploration, and physics demonstrations are shown qualitatively only, with no quantitative assessment of mesh quality, material accuracy under novel lighting, collision/simulation validity, temporal consistency during exploration, or comparison to relevant 3D scene generation/reconstruction systems.

The evidence for PBR material perception is narrow. Roughness and metallic estimation are evaluated mainly on synthetic PanoX, and the authors themselves acknowledge poor generalization for metallic prediction. This is a serious issue because PBR readiness is one of the paper’s headline claims.

Dataset scale and diversity are weaker than the framing suggests: PanoX has only eight source environments and roughly 10k instances. The train/test split by scenes helps, but the dataset may still not support the claimed generalization across diverse indoor/outdoor worlds, materials, and lighting.

Several comparisons raise fairness and reproducibility concerns. Baselines designed for perspective images, video, or different camera models are adapted in ways that are not fully specified, while the proposed method is trained on task-specific synthetic panorama data. It is unclear whether all baselines receive comparable data, resolution, prompting, inference budget, and tuning.

The panorama generation evaluation is incomplete. FID/KID/CLIP-FID/FAED on perspective crops do not adequately measure 360-degree geometric consistency, seam quality, or plausibility of unobserved regions. The qualitative comparisons are limited and selected, and the method is not consistently best across all reported metrics.

The geometry results are mixed despite strong presentation. OmniX is clearly worse than MoGe on distance metrics in Table 4, yet the paper still emphasizes graphics-ready reconstruction. Since distance quality directly determines mesh quality, this limitation should be treated as central rather than secondary.

The application pipeline is underspecified. Important details such as mesh connectivity thresholds, handling of depth discontinuities, UV seams, invalid/infinite depths, material filtering, iterative completion stopping criteria, and accumulated error control are not described sufficiently for reproduction.

The paper lacks a convincing real-world evaluation. In-the-wild results are qualitative, and there is no systematic test on real panoramas with measured geometry/materials or user/visual studies for generated 3D scenes. This leaves a large gap between synthetic benchmark performance and the claimed practical utility.

There are presentation and rigor issues: the project page appears blank in the extracted abstract, some text contains formatting problems, and the results discussion often states superiority more strongly than the tables justify. The limitations section is unusually revealing and confirms several concerns that are not resolved experimentally.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: moving panorama-based 2D lifting beyond RGB appearance toward geometry, intrinsic properties, and PBR-ready 3D scene assets. This is a meaningful contribution for immersive scene generation and graphics/CV pipelines.

OmniX is technically well motivated. Circular synchronization is a clean structural way to handle equirectangular seam consistency, and modality-specific LoRA adapters are a practical design for repurposing strong 2D flow-matching priors across RGB, distance, normals, albedo, roughness, and metallic maps.

The experimental results are broad and generally convincing. The method improves over prior panorama generation baselines on most reported metrics, substantially outperforms intrinsic decomposition baselines on PanoX/Structured3D, and is competitive for geometry despite using less depth supervision than MoGe.

The dataset contribution, PanoX, is valuable: dense aligned panorama annotations for geometry and PBR materials across indoor and outdoor scenes address a real data gap. The out-of-domain scene split is a useful evaluation choice.

Ablations support the main design choices: separate adapters outperform shared alternatives, pretrained generative priors matter, and the supplemental completion results show clear gains over Flux-Fill. The limitations section is unusually candid about depth accuracy, metallic generalization, and the gap between 2D neural priors and PBR rendering.
weaknesses: The strongest application claim, automatic construction of PBR-ready 3D scenes suitable for relighting, simulation, and exploration, is evaluated mainly qualitatively. There is no quantitative assessment of reconstructed mesh quality, relighting/material accuracy, physical-simulation validity, or accumulated error during iterative completion.

PanoX is useful but still limited in diversity: it contains only eight large-scale synthetic environments, and the paper does not fully analyze how scene/source bias affects generalization. The in-the-wild results are qualitative, so real-world robustness remains only partially established.

Several comparisons are potentially uneven. Some baselines are not designed for panoramas or for the same synthetic supervision, while OmniX is trained on task-specific panorama data and multiple adapters. The paper would be stronger with controlled fine-tuning or adaptation baselines under matched data budgets.

Circular synchronization is compelling, but its evidence is mostly visual. A seam-consistency metric, runtime/memory analysis for padded attention, and sensitivity to padding size would make the claim more rigorous.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places: the paper states that 12 adapters are trained on four L40S GPUs, but does not provide enough information about training duration, LoRA ranks, sampling schedules, dataset licensing/release status, or inference cost. The project-page line in the abstract also appears incomplete.

The unified framing is elegant, but the actual system still requires many separately trained adapters for different modalities and masked variants. This weakens the sense of a single unified model and may complicate deployment.
